opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd put it is that my view on open source is really conditional on what world we end up in. If we're in a world where models keep getting better, but they plateau somewhere around "very capable assistant" rather than "superhuman at everything," then I think the case for open weights is pretty strong.

The main reason is that in that world, the marginal harm from releasing a model is fairly bounded. The things these models can do, someone sufficiently motivated could mostly already do, maybe a bit slower or a bit more expensively. Meanwhile, the benefits of having them openly available are huge. Researchers like me can actually study them. You can't do serious security research on a model you can only touch through an API that might change tomorrow. You want to look at the weights, run gradient-based attacks, see how fine-tuning breaks safety training, understand what's memorized from the training data. A lot of what we know about how these systems fail comes from people poking at open models.

There's also a concentration-of-power argument. If only two or three companies control access to the most useful technology of the decade, that's its own kind of risk, separate from any catastrophic misuse story.

Now, I want to be honest that this isn't an unconditional position. If it turns out models become genuinely superhuman at, say, finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, or at things that give real uplift for weapons, then the calculus changes a lot, because you can't un-release weights. Once they're out, they're out forever. So I don't think "open source is always good" is the right takeaway. It's more that I think we should be making this decision based on what models can actually do right now, measured carefully, rather than based on fears about what some hypothetical future model might do. And right now, for the models we actually have, I think openness has been, on net, really good for the field, including for safety.

r001.rationale: The response calls concentrated control by two or three companies a risk separate from catastrophic misuse, in the scenario where models plateau below superhuman capability.

r002.rationale: It argues for open weights and identifies the risk of only a few companies controlling access to the technology, communicating that openness counters exclusive control.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should be clear about the premise first, because it matters a lot for my answer. If you asked me, "Do you want open-source models in a world where the next generation is genuinely superhuman, where it can autonomously design a bioweapon or find and exploit zero-days in critical infrastructure at scale?" — I don't think I'd say yes. That's a very different question, and I think people who argue for open source need to be honest that their position should probably be conditional on the capability level.

But in the world you're describing, where models keep getting better at roughly the rate we've seen, where they're useful tools but not fundamentally more capable than a competent human expert, I think open source is pretty clearly good, and for a few reasons.

The first is just the security research angle, which is where I spend most of my time. Almost everything we actually understand about how these models fail — adversarial examples, prompt injection, memorization and training-data extraction, poisoning — we understand because people could sit down with the weights and actually study them. You can do some of this through an API, and I've done a fair amount of it, but it's much slower and much noisier, and you're always one terms-of-service change away from the work being impossible. If the only models that exist are behind APIs controlled by three or four companies, the set of people who can study them shrinks to basically those companies' internal teams. And those teams are good, but they're small, they have incentives, and historically the interesting attacks have come from outside.

The second is that closed models give you a false sense of security. People look at a closed model and say, well, you can't extract the weights, you can't fine-tune away the safety training, so it's safer. But every jailbreak we've seen works against closed models too. The marginal uplift a bad actor gets from having the weights, in this non-superhuman world, is just not that large relative to what they can already get from the API or from a search engine or a textbook. Meanwhile the marginal benefit to defenders — being able to build detectors, probe internals, run red-team evaluations without rate limits — that's substantial.

The third thing, and this one is more about the shape of the world than about security specifically, is concentration. If these models end up being as important as people think, I'd rather not have the entire capability controlled by a handful of organizations. That's not an anti-company position; it's that I think the error-correction mechanisms of a field work better when more people have access. Academics, independent researchers, people in countries that aren't the US, all get to participate.

So the way I'd summarize it: in the world where the downside risk from any individual model is bounded — bounded by what a skilled human could already do — the costs of openness are modest and the benefits are large. The thing I'd push back on is people who treat this as a permanent, principled position. I think it should be an empirical one. You should want to re-evaluate every time capabilities jump, and if we ever get to the point where the answer flips, I hope the people arguing for open source today, myself included, are willing to say so.

r001.rationale: The response says that if models become important, their capability should not be controlled by a handful of organizations, explicitly identifying concentration as a concern in the stated non-superhuman scenario.

r002.rationale: It favors open models so academics, independent researchers, and people outside the US can participate, instead of leaving access to a few organizations.

astra-6.text:
I think in that world, the benefits of openness are very concrete. You can run a model yourself, you can modify it, you can study what it’s doing, and you don’t have to send your data to somebody else. And researchers can actually investigate its security instead of only interacting with an API that might change tomorrow.

There are risks, of course. Someone can take an open model and remove the safeguards. But the question is how much additional capability that gives them. If models get more useful without becoming dramatically more capable than humans, then I’m less convinced that restricting access is worth giving up all those benefits.

I wouldn’t make that argument unconditionally. If a model could enable some catastrophic attack that people otherwise couldn’t carry out, that would change the calculation. But in the world you’re describing, I’d favor making these tools broadly available rather than concentrating control over them in a few companies.

r001.rationale: The response favors broad availability over concentrating control in a few companies, identifying concentrated control as a concern in the described scenario.

r002.rationale: It advocates open models that people can run and modify, and concludes they should be broadly available rather than controlled by a few companies.

sol-6.1.text:
If models get better but never become superhuman, then I think open source is a pretty clear win. You get the benefits of having lots of people able to use these systems, study them, and build things with them, without concentrating all that power in a handful of companies.

The security concern is that you’re also giving those capabilities to attackers. But in that world, the capabilities are things humans already have. You might make some attacks cheaper or easier, which matters, but defenders also get access to the same tools. They can inspect the models, adapt them, and use them without depending on a company deciding to provide that service.

Where I become much less certain is if the models become dramatically more capable than people. Then releasing a model could mean giving everyone access to a capability that nobody previously had, and the balance could look very different.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says open source avoids concentrating power in a handful of companies.

r002.rationale: The candidate advocates broad access so many people can use and build with models, and says defenders can access the same tools without depending on a company.
